Shambles
SHAM-blz
noun
From the Old English sceamol, “a bench, a stool,” from the Latin scamellum, a little bench — hence the butcher’s bench, the stall on which flesh was cut and sold, and so the meat market itself. It renders the Greek makellon. The modern sense of “a scene of ruin” is a later drift from the slaughter-house.

Biblical Definition

The shambles is the meat market — the butchers’ row, the benches where flesh was cut and sold in a Greek city. In Corinth this was no simple errand. Much of the meat on those benches had been offered first at a heathen altar, the priest taking his portion and the surplus going to the stalls; a Christian housewife buying a joint might well be buying what had lain before an idol that morning. Paul settles it in one line: “whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake: for the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof” (1Co 10:25-26). The ground of the liberty is not indifference but doctrine. An idol is nothing in the world; the beef was never Apollo’s; it was always God’s, for the earth is His and everything in it, and no demon can annex a creature the LORD has made and pronounced good. Buy it, thank God for it, and eat. But Paul does not stop at liberty. If a man tell thee, This is offered in sacrifice unto idols, eat not — not for thine own conscience, but for the other man’s: “Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other” (1Co 10:29). The strong man’s freedom bends before the weak brother’s scruple, for the same apostle who says all things are lawful says all things edify not. Liberty is real, and it is never sovereign; it is a servant, and love is its master.

Webster 1828 Definition

The butchers’ benches; the meat market, where flesh offered to idols was commonly sold.

SHAMBLES, the benches or stalls on which butchers expose flesh for sale; a meat market.

From the Old English sceamol, a bench, from the Latin scamellum.

It renders the Greek makellon, the provision market of a Greek city.

In Corinth much of its meat had first been offered at a heathen altar.

Paul bids the Christian buy and eat, asking no question for conscience sake (1Co 10:25).

Key Scripture

1Co 10:25 — "Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake:"

1Co 10:26 — "For the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof."

1Co 10:29 — "Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other: for why is my liberty judged of another man's conscience?"

Rom 14:14 — "I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean."

Modern Corruption

The age has made conscience sovereign and liberty an end in itself; Paul makes conscience answerable to Scripture and liberty a servant of love.

expand to see more

There is a genuine redefinition here, and it turns on the word conscience. Paul’s conscience is a faculty that must be informed by revelation and can be wrongly bound or wrongly loosed; the age’s conscience is the autonomous self, and “follow your conscience” has come to mean that whatever a man sincerely feels is thereby right and beyond correction. That is not the apostle’s doctrine. He tells the Corinthians why they may eat — because the earth is the Lord’s and the fulness thereof, and an idol is nothing in the world — and the reason is a truth outside the man, not a feeling inside him. A conscience is a window, not a lamp. Scripture alone binds it absolutely; where Scripture has spoken, sincerity is no defence, and where Scripture is silent, no man may forge a chain for his brother.

The shambles cuts both ways, and the church has always been tempted to fall off one side or the other. Legalism looks at the butcher’s bench and forbids what God has not forbidden, making rules where the LORD made meat, and it insults the Creator by conceding to a nothing-idol what belongs to Him. License looks at the same bench, hears the true word that all things are lawful, and marches off to eat in the idol’s temple with a weak brother watching — and so, for a plate of beef, destroys him for whom Christ died. Paul refuses both. Buy in the shambles and ask no questions; but if a man tells you where the meat has been, and his conscience is troubled, put down your fork. The liberty is real and dearly bought, and it is held in trust for the good of the brethren, not spent upon ourselves.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the butchers’ benches, the market where flesh was sold.

Shambles — Old English sceamol, “a bench,” from Latin scamellum.

It denotes the butcher’s stall, and so the meat market itself.

It renders the Greek makellon, the provision market (1Co 10:25).

In Corinth its flesh had commonly been offered first to idols.

The later sense of “a scene of ruin” drifted from the slaughter-house.

Usage

"Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat — for the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof."

"The idol never owned the beef; a nothing cannot annex what God pronounced good."

"If the weak brother’s conscience is told, put down the fork: liberty serves love, and never rules it."
